articles.title: Vance says Ukraine is a ‘partner’ but has some ‘divergent interests’ from US
articles.summary: Vice President Vance said Ukraine is a “partner” but has some “divergent interests” from the U.S. amid tensions between Washington and Kyiv. “Well, they’re certainly a partner in some ways, but I think we, you know, have some divergent interests from time to time,” the vice president said in an interview with 2WAY, talking about…
articles.body:
Vice President Vance said Ukraine is a “partner” but has some “divergent interests” from the U.S. amid tensions between Washington and Kyiv.

“Well, they’re certainly a partner in some ways, but I think we, you know, have some divergent interests from time to time,” the vice president said in an interview with 2WAY, talking about Ukraine.

“Like, for example, do I think they should be bombing Russian diesel facilities that raise the cost of energy for Americans? No. But obviously we’ve worked with them on some things,” Vance added. “We’re going to keep on working with them on some things, but I think they should stop bombing Russian energy.”

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, in an interview with NBC News’s Kristen Welker on “Meet the Press” broadcast Sunday, advised the U.S. that supporting Russian President Vladimir Putin is a “historic mistake.”

“If United States will support Putin, I mean, it’s unbelievable, it’s tragedy, it’s historic mistake and big tragedy. That’s why I think that I don’t want to live in illusions, but I think that we have to be pragmatic,” Zelensky said in the interview.

President Trump went after Zelensky in a Newsmax interview last week. When asked about Ukraine restarting attacks against Russian energy targets despite asking Zelensky to halt such strikes, Trump responded, “Zelensky is not a good guy for us to deal with. I’m not a big fan of Zelensky. They’ve destroyed that country.”

Trump added in the Newsmax interview that he thought the Russia-Ukraine war would “end soon.”

“I think they actually both would like to see it end, but I think I find Zelensky to be more difficult to deal with than Putin,” Trump said.

articles.title: Nigeria confirms first Ebola case amid concerns about continental spread
articles.summary: Nigeria’s Health Ministry says a woman who arrived on a flight from Uganda tested positive.
articles.body:
Nigeria has confirmed its first Ebola case in its capital, Abuja, after a woman who travelled from Uganda tested positive for the virus.

The case in the West African country comes amid an outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo and some cases in Kenya, raising concerns about a spread across the continent.

According to Nigeria’s Federal Ministry of Health and Social Welfare, the woman began showing symptoms on October 7 and was admitted to a private hospital in Abuja on October 11, before being diagnosed with Ebola.

Health Minister Muhammad Pate said authorities had begun trying to trace 44 people who came into contact with the patient.

“We are doing everything possible to contain this case by tracing all the contacts the individual may have had,” he said.

Earlier on Tuesday, Kenya confirmed ⁠its ninth case of Ebola.

A 24-year-old man, who was already being held in quarantine, is the latest to test positive, Kenya’s Ministry of Health said in a statement on Tuesday.

“He was isolated at the first sign of illness, tested and started on treatment immediately upon confirmation of his positive test result,” it said, adding he “was already in quarantine when he fell ill”.

The man was a close family member of Kenya’s first Ebola patient , who had travelled from the DRC, through Uganda and before arriving in Kenya and dying at a Nairobi hospital on ⁠October 5.

“All nine cases belong to one cluster, and as of ‌today there is no evidence of transmission outside this group,” Director-General for Health Patrick Amoth said in a statement on Tuesday.

“Eight patients are stable and responding well to treatment, while 134 of 135 contacts have been traced and quarantined,” Amoth said.

Amoth said a milestone was in sight for the majority of the contacts in quarantine as they had remained well for the 21-day monitoring period and could return home from October 25.

It appealed to communities to welcome them back, saying they “pose no risk of infection”.

The ministry said no infections had occurred within quarantine facilities and that it was continuously monitoring infection-prevention measures to protect health workers.

Despite the nine infections, Kenya has not imposed restrictions on travel, trade or public gatherings, with authorities saying the country remains open for business.

In the DRC, there have been more than 9,000 Ebola cases and 4,000 deaths since May.

The European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control says it’s the second-largest epidemic on record.

It has been difficult to contain because there is no licensed vaccine or specific treatment for the Bundibugyo strain of the virus.

Uganda had previously reported Ebola cases but was later declared free of the virus.

articles.title: UK government to make Jackdaw gas field announcement
articles.summary: The long-awaited decision about the controversial North Sea field is expected on Wednesday morning.
articles.body:
The UK government is expected to announce a long-awaited decision on whether to approve the Jackdaw gas field in the North Sea.

It is widely believed in Westminster that Jackdaw will be approved but that a decision on the Rosebank oil field off Shetland will not yet be made.

The question of whether to approve the two sites has become hugely politically significant and has been delayed for several months.

Multiple Whitehall sources have told BBC News the government would make an announcement on Jackdaw on Wednesday morning with the Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh expected to address MPs in the afternoon.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham has spoken repeatedly of the need for a "flexible" approach to energy and is believed to be in favour of drilling more where licensing already exist in the North Sea.

Labour's 2024 manifesto pledged not to issue any new oil and gas licences in the North Sea but to honour existing ones such as Jackdaw.

Jackdaw, about 150 miles (241.4km) east of Aberdeen, is a gas field which its operators say could be connected to the UK network within months.

Rosebank, about 80 miles (128.7km) north-west of Shetland, is Britain's largest untapped oil field, which would also produce some gas.

The controversial fields have been the subject of years of debates, legal wrangling and public consultations, with arguments from both industry bodies and environmentalists being weighed up by the UK government.

Licences for the fields were granted by the Conservative UK government in 2022 and 2023, which sparked legal challenges from environmental groups.

The Court of Session in Edinburgh ruled last year that Rosebank and Jackdaw had been unlawfully approved because the government had failed to take into account the climate impact of burning extracted oil and gas from the sites.

Environmentalists insist more drilling would be unconscionable, and hamper efforts to cut planet-warming carbon emissions as deadly heatwaves and extreme weather affect people across the globe.

They also claim starting production would not protect energy security and transitioning sooner to greener technologies would be better for supporting jobs.

Industry bodies argue starting production at Rosebank and Jackdaw will provide jobs and improve the UK's energy security as overseas conflicts threaten supply.

articles.title: At the negotiating table and on the battlefield, Russia and Ukraine are at an impasse
articles.summary: It’s like two theatrical performances unfolding side by side, before an audience of one.
articles.body: It’s like two theatrical performances unfolding side by side, before an audience of one. The peace process surrounding Russia’s invasion of Ukraine has reached a remarkable impasse. On one stage, European allies and Kyiv are scrambling to turn US demands and threats into something resembling a plan that might satisfy President Donald Trump. On the other, the Kremlin has its own show: envoy Kirill Dmitriev offers business opportunities designed to appeal to a mercantile US president, draw him further into Moscow’s orbit and allow Russia’s crawling frontline advance to proceed. Trump’s envoys, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, flit between the two productions. Yet the two plots remain separate and contemptuous of each other, with no denouement in sight. When Trump speaks of a deal with Russia, one fact outweighs all others: Moscow’s idea of peace is basically victory. The Kremlin has been blunt about its demands, even in their least maximalist form. Russian President Vladimir Putin wants Ukraine to surrender the Donbas without further fighting. He has also long entertained Ukraine’s demilitarization, a pledge never to join NATO and a change of leadership in Kyiv — all impractical or impossible in wartime. Russia’s pragmatist-in-chief has therefore settled on the Donbas as an attainable negotiating goal, while pressure grows on Kyiv to concede. Why does Zelensky not simply yield? Reasons to do so grow as what remains of the Donbas becomes less habitable by the day. Russian drones stalk Kramatorsk, the largest population center, hunting civilians around the clock. Sloviansk, Dobropillia and Kostyantynivka are either ruins or targets for Russian glide bombs: places of great military importance, but little remaining civilian life. Yet the clearest case for why Ukraine cannot simply abandon the Donbas came from none other than Trump’s National security adviser, and possible successor, Marco Rubio. Russia controls all but 11% of the Donetsk region, while Ukraine describes the remainder as the “defensive line that they’ve embedded themselves in,” he said, in an interview with Breitbart News. “They argue, and military strategists say is true, that it is the last defensible line… From there, it’s just a straight shot into Kyiv.” He added that Russia is not really advancing and has therefore switched to “applying extraordinary pain on the people of Ukraine through drone strikes, through ballistic missile strikes, trying to destroy their energy infrastructure, their electricity.” Ukraine, in turn, is striking Russian refineries. He acknowledged Kushner and Witkoff’s efforts, but ultimately concluded: “We’d like the war to end, but ultimately we also have other priorities around the world we’re focused on as well.” Rubio spent 45 minutes on the phone with Zelensky on Tuesday, suggesting he may be more invested in the outcome than this closing remark implies. But his lowered expectations reflect the reality of these two separate onstage peace performances. Ukraine wants to survive; Russia wants to win, and still believes it can. If one of the sounder minds in the White House sees peace as a long shot at best, what did the past 10 days of US-Ukrainian fallout achieve? Did it get Trump any closer to the deal he says he wants? Trump has offered a striking array of pro-Russian incentives to draw Moscow towards a peace whose terms he has yet to define. It looks like pressure for its own sake — and to Putin’s immediate advantage. The list of Trump gifts to Moscow is extensive: a sudden diesel deal likely to throw billions into Putin’s war chest; an energy ceasefire (unilaterally announced by Trump and apparently unknown to either side), that slowed Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries for several days. There were also restrictions on vital Starlink technology that affected Ukraine’s defensive and offensive operations; limits on intelligence sharing that left Ukraine without warning of ballistic missile attacks for at least several nights; and repeated calls for Zelensky to leave office. Add to that the monthslong collapse of US financial support for Ukraine, with Europe now paying for military aid. If Putin could write US policy, it might look much like this. Speaking in a news conference in Oslo after meeting with Witkoff in person and Kushner virtually, Zelensky said he hoped for a positive word from Rubio soon on the US-made Patriot air defense system and Starlink, while also saying that his country was “thankful that intelligence sharing” with the United States “now works.” Witkoff heads to Russia tomorrow and the nature of what he will present to Putin remains unclear. Why now? The political damage Trump is inflicting on himself and his Republican colleagues ahead of the midterms is palpable. Some are struggling to distance themselves from this profoundly anti-American barrage of pro-Russian policies. Equally striking is how unsustainable or impractical many of these measures are. The diesel deal will not lower US pump prices quickly and European restrictions, will probably limit how much cash it can deliver to Putin. The energy ceasefire was brief, absurd, and further undermined Trump’s credibility. Restrictions to Starlink, Starshield, the military-grade version of Starlink controlled by the US government, and intelligence sharing appear to come and go, leaving Ukrainian troops in the lurch, while Rubio echoes Trump’s denial that any such limits ever existed. This flurry of baffling activity makes sense only when seen through the US political prism. It is addressing the world after the midterm elections. Zelensky has dispensed with the canard that pandering to Trump works. Ukraine is emotionally more adjusted to the idea of losing US support and going it alone, aware that survival is preferable to friendship with a fickle US. Europe knows there is a limited window now left in which Trump can do damage, and that whatever comes next is better. Even if it is more of the same, at least Europe and Ukraine will have had longer to prepare to go it alone. Most troubling is Trump’s timing and thinking. He is only doing damage to his party and legacy. But with Republicans still in control of the House and Senate, and 2028’s race to succeed him not yet begun in earnest, perhaps he sees this as his last unbridled moment to express in practical ways his sympathy to someone apparently oddly important to him, as a US president: Vladimir Putin.

articles.title: Sea mine crisis re-emerges in Strait of Hormuz as Tehran urges Washington to accept deal
articles.summary: Iran claims two oil tankers struck sea mines in the Strait of Hormuz as the IMO warns the critical shipping lane remains too unsafe to transit.
articles.body: Sea mines have resurfaced as a threat in the Strait of Hormuz, where Iran claimed Oct.17 that two oil tankers caught fire after striking the explosives, raising fresh alarms over the safety of one of the world's most critical shipping lanes. This came as the International Maritime Organization (IMO) warned that sea mines pose a serious threat to vessels navigating the strategic waterway and while Tehran continues to maintain its own unauthorized shipping corridor inside its territorial waters. "The traffic separation scheme, the information that we have is that they still have mines. And of course, whilst the conflict is ongoing, it's very difficult for us to use third parties to verify that it is clear of these hazards," IMO Secretary-General Arsenio Dominguez told Fox News Digital. INSIDE THE DANGEROUS US MISSION THAT CLEARED IRAN’S MINES FROM HORMUZ SHIPPING LANES "So in the meantime, we cannot guarantee that a vessel that intends to transit that route will not be hit by a mine." Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) navy said Saturday that two oil tankers caught fire after striking naval mines while crossing the Strait of Hormuz, Reuters reported, citing Iran's official Islamic Republic News Agency (IRNA). State media also said both tankers were carrying about 2 million barrels of crude oil, according to Reuters. IRNA also reported that the vessels had switched off their positioning and radar systems and attempted to use a route through the strategic waterway that Iran had not authorized. IRAN WARNS SHIPS OF 'FORCEFUL RESPONSE' AS US-BACKED HORMUZ ROUTE CHALLENGES TEHRAN'S GRIP The second tanker was left immobilized after striking a mine, according to the Reuters report. The alleged strikes came as Tehran continued to maintain its transit passageway inside Iranian territorial waters, imposing tolls and safety fees administered by the IRGC — a framework rejected by Washington and the IMO as inconsistent with international maritime law. International shipping through the narrow chokepoint has historically relied on an IMO-approved traffic separation scheme adopted in 1968. "Right now there's only one route that was adopted back in 1968 that is approved and recognized for IMO and that appears in all the charts for the vessels to operate," Dominguez explained. IRAN FAILS TO STRIKE DEAL WITH US AS DEADLINE PASSES AND TRUMP CALLS FOR ‘WHITE FLAG OF SURRENDER' "There's only one route that should be used for transit, but it's not clear of mines right now, so it's not safe." "We have received confirmation from Iran about the establishment of its temporary route in the waters," he added before stating that the route was not provided with "an official confirmation or a decision of the organization." "Any other route needs to actually be sent to the organization to go through the processes, and we have not received that." "We have received communication from Iran to use that route because of the conflict," Dominguez clarified. "That's the way that it's been presented. But anything for us to approve needs to go through the mechanisms at the international maritime organizations and the member states need to review it." The developments also came amid stalled negotiations between Washington and Tehran over ending the conflict and restoring maritime traffic. DISTRESS CALL CAPTURES TANKER UNDER FIRE, IRAN SHUTS HORMUZ TRAPPING THOUSANDS OF SAILORS Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council and a former Revolutionary Guard commander, said Tehran considered Washington's latest response to negotiations "insufficient," Reuters reported, according to IRNA. Rezaei said the U.S. had accepted some of Iran's seven conditions but that other issues remained unresolved, adding that Tehran was no longer responding to Washington and that the U.S. needed to clarify the outstanding matters. Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said that Tehran had submitted a proposal to Washington through Qatar, which is mediating the negotiations, outlining conditions under which the Strait of Hormuz could reopen and normal maritime traffic resume within seven days. "Our situation is clear and based on ⁠the seven-day proposal presented to the US. They shared comments which ​we are reviewing, but our proposal is still on the table ​and if there is any honesty on the US part, which there isn't, the way to reopening the Strait of Hormuz is obvious," Araqchi said in ​Baghdad, Reuters reported IRAN REQUESTS TALKS WITH US AS WHITE HOUSE WARNS 'VIOLENCE WILL BE MET WITH VIOLENCE' Meanwhile, attacks on commercial vessels around the Strait of Hormuz have surged over the past two weeks. Senior Iranian officials also told Reuters that Tehran has shifted its strategy for attacking commercial vessels during that period. For commercial shipping operators, Dominguez warned that the continued threat of mines and attacks means the waterway has yet to return to normal operations. The Strait of Hormuz is "not open for business in the way that it was before the conflict started," he said. "Our role right now is to prepare for when we have the opportunity to go back, resume the operations, follow all the procedures at IMO, but not until the root causes are addressed and those are beyond IMO." articles.summary: The EA says the lake requires improvements to "reduce the risk of life" caused by potential floods.
articles.body:
A lake is failing safety standards and requires improvements worth more than £1m to "reduce the risk of life" posed by a potential flood.

The Environment Agency (EA) has served an enforcement notice to Gateshead Council over the condition of the lake at Watergate Forest Park.

The notice means the authority must reduce the risk of the lake overflowing during extreme rain by February in order to avoid being taken to court.

The Reform-UK led authority said the works required would be carried out in the coming months.

The local authority's leader Nick Allan repeatedly branded the EA the "flat earth society" at a council meeting.

He said carrying out the works themselves would be "significantly more cost effective" than potentially facing penalties from the agency, according to the Local Democracy Reporting Service .

But he questioned the fact that only contractors Esh had bid for the council scheme and the fact the costs of the repairs had jumped from an original £400,000 estimate to £1.2m.

Reform councillor Graham Keating said something was not "working properly" if only one company had come through the North East Procurement Organisation (NEPO) framework.

The authority's head Dale Owens said NEPO was "well proven" to offer savings to local councils and explained that the cost increase was due to various factors, including inflation.

Allan said he had tried to stop the contract being awarded to Esh but it had been too late.

He said he did not think the "financial interests of the council were being served by the current procurement process.

The works will include a reinforcement of the reservoir's existing spillway using asphalt and additional concrete protection measures designed to accommodate a one-in-10,000-year flood event.

The lake was designated as a reservoir in 2021.

articles.body: The popular grocery store Trader Joe's is expanding with 30 new locations across 16 states. Two of the stores — in Anaheim Hills, California, and West Jordan, Utah — are set to open this week, according to Trader Joe's website. The other 28, which span states from Arizona to Washington, are listed as "coming soon." "We are actively looking at hundreds of neighborhoods across the country as we hope to open more new neighborhood stores each year," the spokesperson told Fox News Digital. "Since Trader Joe's began in 1967, we have been in growth mode," the spokesperson added. articles.title: A former soldier pulled a 1.5-tonne Land Rover for 100 km in 100 hours; he was trying to raise £100,000 for families with a rare brain disease
articles.summary: A former British soldier took an extraordinary test of strength and endurance by pulling a 1.5-tonne Land Rover across 100 kilometres in 100 hours.
articles.body: A former British soldier took an extraordinary test of strength and endurance by pulling a 1.5-tonne Land Rover across 100 kilometres in 100 hours. Darren Hardy, an extreme athlete from Fleet in Hampshire, launched the challenge to raise £100,000 for research into a rare and incurable brain disease affecting children. His efforts were focused on helping 17-year-old Aggie Candy-Waters and other families living with hypomyelination with atrophy of the basal ganglia and cerebellum, commonly known as H-ABC.Former soldier pulling a 1.5-tonne Land Rover for 100 kmAccording to Hobbs Independent, Hardy's challenge was designed to set a world record for the furthest distance a vehicle has been pulled. The attempt was scheduled to begin at noon on 20 March 2026 at Blackbushe Airport in Camberley, Hampshire. The goal was to cover 100 kilometres within 100 hours, demanding sustained physical effort rather than a short burst of strength.The Dunsfold Collection described the attempt as Hardy's biggest challenge yet. The distance was more than two marathons, but the difficulty extended beyond covering the ground. The challenge was to keep moving while managing exhaustion, changing weather conditions and the physical strain of dragging a heavy vehicle.Hardy explained that the challenge requires careful attention to food and hydration. He expected to consume approximately 45,000 calories and drink around 50 litres of water and electrolytes during the 100-hour attempt.The rare brain disease behind the fundraising effortThe money raised through the challenge was intended to support the H-ABC Foundation and SynaptixBio, a UK biotechnology company developing a potential treatment for the condition. As reported by Hobbs Independent, H-ABC is a severe form of TUBB4a leukodystrophy, a genetic condition that affects the central nervous system. It is rare, progressive and currently has no approved cure.Hardy's commitment to the cause began in 2019, when he came across the story of Aggie Candy-Waters. Her experience motivated him to use his endurance challenges to support research that could improve the lives of children affected by the disease.The Dunsfold Collection reported that Hardy raised more than £120,000 through his previous charitable efforts. This attempt was aimed to generate another £100,000 specifically for work that could help make treatment more accessible to patients and their families.A safer way to deliver treatment is importantSynaptixBio is developing an antisense oligonucleotide therapy for H-ABC. According to Hobbs Independent, preclinical studies had indicated that the treatment could halt disease progression and potentially reverse some symptoms. The company selected a lead candidate, identified as SB H-19642, and had been working towards clinical trials, potentially in early 2027.However, developing a potential treatment is only part of the challenge. Delivering it safely into the body is another important consideration, particularly because many people affected by H-ABC are young children.The funds from Hardy's challenge had been earmarked for developing a safer and simpler delivery method. The approach involves injecting medicine directly into the cerebrospinal fluid, a procedure that presents risks and practical difficulties.Researchers hope to develop a method that would allow the drug to be administered intravenously, through a vein. Such an approach could make treatment easier to deliver while avoiding the challenges associated with direct injection into the fluid surrounding the brain and spinal cord.Hobbs Independent reported that SynaptixBio had received a £2 million BioMedical Catalyst grant from Innovate UK. The company also received Rare Paediatric Disease Designations from the US Food and Drug Administration for H-ABC and related conditions.The Land Rover collection supported the attemptThe challenge had also brought together an unusual piece of automotive history. The Dunsfold Collection lended Hardy two prototype Land Rovers built in 1981. Only four were originally made, and just two have survived.One vehicle was supposed to be used for Hardy's record attempt, while the second was for other participants to pull alongside him. This arrangement gave members of the public an opportunity to take part in the event rather than simply watch from the sidelines.Hardy's military past and commitment to charityHardy's determination to take on physically demanding challenges developed after a difficult period in his life. According to The Dunsfold Collection, he was medically discharged from the Army in 2017 after experiencing complex post-traumatic stress disorder, following incidents in Iraq and a training exercise in Canada.He subsequently channelled his energy into extreme physical challenges for charitable causes and founded StayStrong. His previous efforts had included pulling a car for 50 kilometres, running 317 kilometres over 92 hours and completing multiple marathons within short periods.These achievements helped him raise money for H-ABC research while drawing attention to the families affected by the condition. Since Hardy began supporting the cause, SynaptixBio had been established and attracted £11 million in additional investment towards treatment development. The 100-kilometre Land Rover pull was another step in his continuing efforts to support children living with H-ABC.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Trump finds ominous campaign message in French riots
articles.summary: President Trump is issuing an ominous message to supporters, warning that Democratic control of Congress would lead to chaos and destruction in his closing midterm pitch two weeks out from Election Day. Trump sought to tie the protests and riots rocking France to the U.S. during a rally in Kansas on Monday, saying the U.S.…
articles.body:
President Trump is issuing an ominous message to supporters, warning that Democratic control of Congress would lead to chaos and destruction in his closing midterm pitch two weeks out from Election Day.

Trump sought to tie the protests and riots rocking France to the U.S. during a rally in Kansas on Monday, saying the U.S. could face a similar scenario with Democratic majorities on Capitol Hill.

“To see what is at stake in this election, just look at what’s happening in France,” Trump told supporters.

Vice President Vance sent a similar message on Monday in response to a post on the social platform X with a video showing a 150-year-old town hall burning in France.

“I pray that France, a beautiful country of amazing people, will stop this madness before more of its landmarks burn,” he wrote. “And I hope Americans are paying attention. This is the future congressional Democrats seek for your country.”

Speaking in the Oval Office on Tuesday, Trump sounded off about the riots that have gripped France.

“When you look at France, and it happened in Italy too, smaller scale, but it’s right there, it’s simmering,” Trump said, pointing to immigrants as the driving force of the protests, which began with teenage students pushing for better schools.

“If you don’t get that out, and you’re going to have to remove the people, you’re going to have to remove those people that are insurrectionists,” he added, drawing a contrast with his own hard-line border policies.

While the messaging could provide useful fodder to galvanize Trump’s conservative base, it could turn off Independent voters, who are displeased with the state of the economy under the Trump administration and Republican control of Congress.

“It’s somewhat delusional, even dangerously delusional to think that a riot in France will supersede the economic needs and priorities of Americans two weeks out from an election,” said one Republican strategist.

Trump’s focus on France comes as Republican candidates remain focused on economic messaging — with many looking for distance from the president’s least popular policies.

“All Republicans need to be focused on is restoring confidence with swing voters who are abandoning the party due [to] our failure to focus on economic issues. Failure to do so will lead to disappointment on election night,” said Paul Shumaker, a North Carolina-based Republican strategist.

A Reuters/Ipsos poll released Tuesday found that 68 percent of respondents, including 37 percent of self-identified Republicans, said they disapproved of Trump’s handling of the economy.

The president has talked frequently about the economy in his final midterm blitz, touting the One Big Beautiful Bill Act. On Monday, Trump made headlines when he announced an $8 billion relief program for farmers negatively impacted by high diesel prices.

Trump indicated that the protests in France will remain part of his economic messaging in the days ahead.

“When I go to North Carolina, today I’m going to be speaking about it. But Europe has to change its ways or you’re not going to have Europe left,” Trump told reporters in the Oval Office on Tuesday ahead of a campaign rally in Greenville, N.C.

The unrest in France initially began with protests over the summer focused on teacher shortages and declining building conditions. The protests then quickly spread to other parts of the country, and fringe riots have since emerged.

In a statement to The Hill, deputy White House press secretary Anna Kelly said Trump’s warnings over Europe are nothing new and are meant to protect the U.S.

“These destructive policies have made once-great European cities unrecognizable — allowing crime and antisemitic violence to run rampant and posing an unsustainable cost on social safety net programs,” Kelly said.

“The president saved the United States from such destruction when he was elected, and he has rightfully warned Americans of the chaos that awaits if Democrats allow the same radical left lunatics to wreak havoc on our communities,” she continued.

Trump also sees the unrest in Europe as an opportunity to highlight his own immigration record as he seeks to galvanize his base. The president attacked the Somali community in Minnesota, as well as the Haitian community in Springfield during a rally in Ohio.

The president’s use of dark and menacing language at campaign rallies is hardly new. During the launch of his first presidential campaign in 2015, the president accused Mexican migrants crossing the U.S. southern border of being “rapists” and bringing drugs and crime into the U.S.

“He does fire and brimstone,” the unnamed Republican strategist said. “But after being solely in power for two years, it just doesn’t work.”

The president’s rhetoric mirrors that of his past messaging ahead of the 2018 midterms, in which he warned of a migrant caravan threatening the U.S., as well as in 2020, when he attacked demonstrators following the police killing of George Floyd.

While the messaging has helped mobilize MAGA voters in the past, polls suggest Trump and his party could be headed for major losses in two weeks.

“Trump’s instinct, of course, is to scare people,” Republican strategist Rob Stutzman said. “When you are at record-low disapproval ratings, there probably isn’t much point in being aspirational.”

The same Reuters/Ipsos poll found that Trump’s approval rating hit a record low of 31 percent.

“But having said that, Americans remember unrest in major American cities,” Stutzman said, referring to the unrest following Floyd’s death and during the pandemic.

“And the failure to secure the southern border is probably the most glaring, enduring ineptitude of the Biden administration,” he continued.

Stutzman argued that Trump’s line of attack on the French riots could help with base turnout.

“It’s the type of rhetoric and fear and demagoguery that helped him build his coalition of unique, otherwise disengaged voters,” he said.

articles.title: Woman accused of holding stepson captive over 20 years in abusive conditions to go to trial in February
articles.summary: Kimberly Sullivan’s 32-year-old stepson told police last year he had spent almost his entire life being abused, starved and held in captivity, according to an affidavit.
articles.body: The case of a Connecticut woman accused of holding her stepson captive for over two decades is expected to go to trial in February. A judge at the Waterbury Judicial District courthouse received a series of confidential records in the case against Kimberly Sullivan during a hearing on Tuesday. Sullivan wasn’t present at the hearing. Over the next several weeks, the judge is expected to review the records obtained via a state subpoena from the Department of Children and Families, the Waterbury Public Schools and an undisclosed treatment facility. He will then determine which ones can be used during the trial. Sullivan’s case drew national attention after shocking details around the allegations that her stepson had been living in captivity since he was 11 began to emerge following her arrest in March 2025. According to an affidavit, Sullivan’s 32-year-old stepson told police that he had spent almost his entire life being abused, starved and held in captivity — prompting him to intentionally start a fire in his room in order to regain his freedom. At the home, police found the man severely malnourished, noting he had not received medical or dental care in years and had been subjected to “prolonged abuse, starvation, severe neglect and inhumane treatment,” according to police. At the time of Sullivan’s arrest, her 5-foot-9 stepson weighed 68 pounds. “It was worse than the conditions of a jail cell,” Waterbury Police Chief Fernando Spagnolo told reporters last year of the man’s living situation. In April 2025, Waterbury police released dozens of photos from inside the home through a Freedom of Information request to NBC Connecticut, showing rooms cluttered with items, walls covered in smoke and destroyed from the fire, and doors with locks on the outside. Ioannis Kaloidis, Sullivan’s attorney, decried the release of the images at the time, telling NBC Connecticut that the move by police was “shocking, offensive and quite frankly, ethically questionable” and threatened his client’s right to “a fair trial.” Sullivan pleaded not guilty to charges of kidnapping, assault, unlawful restraint and intentional cruelty to persons. Sullivan also rejected two different plea deals in September: one offered by the judge, granting her a 30-year sentence to be suspended after serving 10 years, and another one from the state. The latter one included 30 years in prison, suspended after 20 years served, and five years of probation. Kaloidis has said his client has consistently “maintained her innocence.” During Tuesday’s hearing, Kaloidis filed a series of motions, including a request for a 12-member jury, instead of six, and another one asking state prosecutors not to refer to Sullivan’s stepson as “the victim” during the trial. The first motion will be argued in the next court hearing set for Nov. 23. The judge granted the second one on Tuesday. Sullivan’s stepson, who is only identified in court by the alias S., is expected to testify during the trial, NBC Connecticut reported. The judge granted a motion filed by Kaloidis on Tuesday requesting that all information that could potentially challenge or undermine the credibility of S. and his sister, who is also expected to testify, be shared during the pretrial discovery phase. If convicted next year, Sullivan faces more than 45 years in prison. Jury selection for February’s trial is expected to begin about a month before.

articles.title: Trump teases release of Stephen Hubbard, American man jailed in Russia
articles.summary: President Trump on Tuesday said he’s asked Russian President Vladimir Putin to release jailed American Stephen Hubbard, teasing that a resolution could happen within a few days. “Remember that question for a couple of days from now,” Trump said when asked about reports claiming the U.S. was closing in on a deal for Hubbard’s release. …
articles.body:
President Trump on Tuesday said he’s asked Russian President Vladimir Putin to release jailed American Stephen Hubbard, teasing that a resolution could happen within a few days.

“Remember that question for a couple of days from now,” Trump said when asked about reports claiming the U.S. was closing in on a deal for Hubbard’s release.

“I’ve been talking to President Putin about Mr. Hubbard. I’ve been talking to him at length. I’ve asked him to release him,” the president continued.

Trump’s top envoy for peace negotiations, Steve Witkoff, is expected to travel to Moscow this week as part of efforts to move forward negotiations to end Russia’s war against Ukraine.

ABC News on Tuesday reported that Witkoff, along with Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner, are leading the negotiations for Hubbard’s release alongside their talks to make a deal to end the war.

The State Department considers Hubbard, 74, “wrongfully detained.” He was reportedly arrested by Russian forces from his home in eastern Ukraine in 2022 during Russia’s full-scale invasion of the country.

The New York Times reported that Hubbard was accused by Russia of manning a checkpoint and fighting for Ukraine. He was convicted in October 2024 of being a mercenary and sentenced to almost seven years in a penal colony.

The U.S. determination that Hubbard is “wrongfully detained” signals that the administration believes the charges against him are unfounded.

Trump relishes his involvement in securing the release of Americans and others unjustly detained abroad. His administration counts more than 100 Americans he’s helped leave foreign jails.

In August, the administration celebrated Russia’s release of American Robert Gilman from a Russian jail, and brought up the administration’s efforts to secure Hubbard’s release.

“We are still seeking the immediate return of all other unjustly detained Americans, including wrongful detainee Stephen Hubbard. The President will not stop until all unjustly detained Americans are home,” the State Department said in a statement at the time.

The talks for Hubbard’s release come as Trump has extended concessions to Russia by offering to purchase diesel and waive sanctions required by federal law, explaining his moves as keeping Putin at the negotiating table.

In a post on Truth Social, Trump said, “Great progress is being made, that includes the current hostage negotiations!”

But Trump’s outreach to Putin has triggered escalating blowback from Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, European partners, Democrats and an increasing number of Republicans in Congress.

Still, Trump has rejected the criticism, and he is turning the blame on Zelensky as failing to come to a deal with Russia to end the war.

“Ukraine has to want to settle this war, Zelensky has to want to settle this war, and if he doesn’t, I think it’s going to be a very bad thing,” Trump said.

articles.title: EU revises Arctic strategy as pressure from Russia, US grows
articles.summary: The new strategy shifts the bloc’s focus from long-term climate concerns to urgent security measures.
articles.body:
The European Commission has unveiled a new Arctic strategy for the European Union that lists security and resilience first among four priorities, alongside climate change, economic prosperity and opportunities for Arctic communities.

The strategy calls for a new maritime security hub to help member states and partners share information and monitor maritime activity in the Arctic, the Commission said on Tuesday.

The hub would later expand to track shadow fleet vessels, detect illegal fishing and pollution, and improve search and rescue coordination.

The Commission also said the EU will work to expand European icebreaker capacity. Icebreakers are specialised vessels designed to navigate ice-covered waters by breaking up sea ice and maintaining safe shipping routes.

“The Arctic is one place where the tectonic plates of geopolitics are colliding,” European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said, adding that sovereignty and territorial integrity can no longer be taken for granted.

EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said Russia is expanding its military footprint in the high north, citing drone incursions, GPS jamming and cable sabotage, the AFP news agency reported.

Several measures appear aimed at reducing dependence on the United States . The Commission said the EU will back a strategic pan-Arctic fibre-optic telecommunications cable project linking Greenland directly to Europe. It is part of a wider plan that would also connect Canada, Japan and South Korea.

The EU will also provide secure satellite connectivity for government communications through the IRIS² constellation, a constellation AFP said is meant to rival US tech mogul Elon Musk’s Starlink .

The shift follows US President Donald Trump’s repeated demands to take control of Greenland , a Danish autonomous territory. Although his tone has softened this year, with a security deal signed with Greenland and Denmark, many in Europe remain wary, AFP said.

The strategy follows last month’s meeting of leaders from 12 countries, including Germany, France, Finland and Denmark. Member states urged the EU to take a more strategic and proactive role, according to a joint statement.

Participants identified Russia as the largest threat while noting the ambitions of China and the US.

At the meeting, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said the era of “high north, low attention” was over. Finnish Prime Minister Petteri Orpo called Russia the most significant long-term threat and said the EU must treat the Arctic as a strategic frontier.

The Commission reiterated the EU’s position remains that oil, coal and gas should stay in the ground, including in the Arctic.

To combat increasing climate concerns, the Commission pledged to “strengthen climate research, observation and monitoring to better understand these changes and support effective responses”, while working in tandem with the people who live and work in the Arctic.

articles.title: Musk ordered Starlink slowdown in Ukraine: WSJ
articles.summary: Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk ordered the slowdown of Starshield, the military version of Starlink internet, which Ukraine said hampered its ability to respond to Russian attacks, the Wall Street Journal reported, citing U.S. officials and people familiar with the matter. The disruption impacted Ukraine’s drones, airplanes and helicopters, a source familiar with the…
articles.body:
Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk ordered the slowdown of Starshield, the military version of Starlink internet, which Ukraine said hampered its ability to respond to Russian attacks, the Wall Street Journal reported, citing U.S. officials and people familiar with the matter.

The disruption impacted Ukraine’s drones, airplanes and helicopters, a source familiar with the matter previously told The Hill.

Musk initially said in a post to the social platform X, which he owns, that only President Trump or the U.S. military could have ordered the slowdown. While Starlink is a product of Musk’s SpaceX, Starshield is owned and operated by the U.S. government, Musk said last week.

A representative for Musk and the White House did not immediately respond to The Hill’s requests for comment.

The move comes as both Trump and Musk are increasingly critical of Ukraine and its president, Volodymyr Zelensky. Zelensky said after the slowdown that “people will die” and called the move a “big mistake.”

In recent weeks, Trump has called for Ukraine to get a new president , signed an executive order waiving sanctions on Russian energy and purchased hundreds of thousands of tons of Russian diesel, which Democrats and some Republicans bashed as funding Russia’s ability to wage war on Ukraine.

Trump also threatened to stop sharing intelligence with Kyiv if Ukraine continues its attacks on Russian energy infrastructure. The president has criticized Ukraine for those attacks as he grapples with rising energy costs in the U.S. While gas prices have risen as a direct result of the U.S. war with Iran, Trump has blamed Ukraine in recent weeks.

Members of both parties have slammed the administration for its actions on Ukraine. Congress overwhelmingly passed a sanctions package against Russia named for the late Sen. Lindsey Graham (R-S.C.). Graham’s sister Darline, who now holds his Senate seat, said over the weekend that she thinks Trump should keep pressure on Russia.

“Personally, I would choose to keep the pressure on Russia … because I don’t trust Putin, and I don’t trust Russia,” Graham said.

articles.title: Man, 26, charged with woman's murder
articles.summary: Lawrence Johnson has been charged with the murder of Alisha Samuels who died on Thursday.
articles.body:
A man has been charged with the murder of a woman who was stabbed to death in a street in Manchester.

Lawrence Johnson, 26, of Dorking Avenue, has been charged with the murder of Alisha Samuels, also 26, and the attempted murder of a man following the incident on Thursday.

He has been remanded in custody and is due to appear at Manchester Magistrates' Court on Wednesday.

Det Ch Insp Justin Bryant said officers were continuing to investigate the circumstances surrounding Ms Samuels' death and to provide answers for her family.

Police are still appealing for information.

Det Ch Insp Bryant said: "I'd like to thank those that have called and supported our investigation thus far. Your reports are always taken seriously and prove vital to our work.

"I urge others who may have information, no matter how small, to please come forward."

articles.title: In 1858, a Texas family began holding ranchland that developers later wanted for 3,500 houses; in 2016, the family backed a plan to preserve 204 acres for a San Antonio park worth nearly $10 million

articles.body: A century-and-a-half-old family ranch in northern San Antonio became the focus of a major conservation effort in June 2016, when the Classen-Steubing family agreed to sell 204 acres of largely undeveloped land to the city for a future park and protection of the Edwards Aquifer. The proposal, reported by Texas Public Radio and the San Antonio Express-News, offered an alternative to a residential development that could have brought as many as 3,500 homes and apartments to the site. The planned acquisition covered part of the historic Classen-Steubing Ranch in the Stone Oak area, one of the remaining large undeveloped tracts on San Antonio’s North Side. City officials viewed the deal as an opportunity to preserve open space while safeguarding an important source of drinking water. Scroll down to read more.A family decision shaped by conservationThe ranch had been in the Classen-Steubing family since 1858. As development expanded across northern San Antonio, the future of the property became a question of whether to retain its natural character or allow housing to transform the landscape.The family ultimately supported a plan that balanced preservation with limited recreational development. Rather than permitting the entire tract to be built over, the agreement would place most of the land under public ownership and protect it from conventional residential construction.San Antonio officials said the proposed purchase would prevent thousands of potential housing units from being built on the property. The decision also offered a way to preserve the landscape for future generations as residential growth put increasing pressure on open land in the region.Protecting the Edwards AquiferA central reason for the acquisition was the property’s location over the Edwards Aquifer recharge zone. Rainwater entering this area can replenish the underground water system, which supplies drinking water to San Antonio and surrounding communities.Conserving land above the recharge zone helps limit the effects of development, including the construction of roads, roofs and other surfaces that can reduce the amount of rainfall entering the ground. The city’s conservation strategy therefore extended beyond creating a public park.Officials considered the purchase an investment in water protection, with the undeveloped portion of the ranch offering an opportunity to retain natural ground cover in a rapidly urbanising area. The proposal also received support from local conservation advocates, who viewed the property as particularly valuable because of its recharge potential.A two-stage plan for a 204-acre parkThe city structured the proposed acquisition in two parts, separating the land intended primarily for conservation from the portion planned for active recreation. Under the arrangement presented to the City Council, San Antonio would purchase approximately 165 acres for about $6.35 million, plus closing costs. Funding would largely come from a voter-approved Edwards Aquifer protection programme, alongside redirected municipal funds.The remaining 39 acres would be covered by an option to purchase for approximately $3.79 million, with the possibility of using funding from the city’s 2017 bond programme. The overall acquisition was expected to cost close to $10 million. While the larger section would remain predominantly natural open space, the smaller recreational area could accommodate sports fields, walking and cycling trails, and other park facilities.City Council approves the initial purchaseOn June 16, 2016, San Antonio’s City Council approved the initial 165-acre acquisition and the option covering the additional 39 acres. The arrangement also included provisions for a conservation easement and related infrastructure improvements.The phased approach allowed the city to begin protecting the most environmentally sensitive land while leaving the remaining purchase subject to a separate funding decision.
